slides.heading: Two Number Sum
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Two Number Sum, an easy arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Given distinct integers and a target, return any pair summing to the target (empty array if none).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Given distinct integers and a target, return any pair summing to the target (empty array if none).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: For each number x, we need to know if its partner, target minus x, has already appeared.
A hash set answers that instantly.
slides.narration: For each number x, we need to know if its partner, target minus x, has already appeared. A hash set answers that instantly.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: check every pair → O(n²)
Sorting + two pointers → O(n log n), O(1) space
Hash set of seen values → O(n) time, O(n) space
slides.narration: The brute force checks every pair, which is n squared. Sorting and using two pointers gets n log n with constant extra space. The hash-set approach is linear: for each number, we just ask whether its partner has already appeared.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Walk the array once
2. Check whether target minus x is in the set
3. If so, return the pair
4. Otherwise add x to the set
slides.narration: Step by step. First, walk the array once. Second, check whether target minus x is in the set. Third, if so, return the pair. Fourth, otherwise add x to the set.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: array = [3, 5, -4, 8, 11, 1, -1, 6], target = 10
slides.narration: Let's trace the array three, five, minus four, eight, eleven, one, minus one, six, with a target of ten.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 7 not seen yet → remember 3
slides.narration: At index 0 the value is 3, so we need 7. It isn't in the set yet, so we add 3 and move on.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 14 not seen yet → remember -4
slides.narration: At index 2 the value is -4, so we need 14. It isn't in the set yet, so we add -4 and move on.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 2 not seen yet → remember 8
slides.narration: At index 3 the value is 8, so we need 2. It isn't in the set yet, so we add 8 and move on.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: -1 not seen yet → remember 11
slides.narration: At index 4 the value is 11, so we need -1. It isn't in the set yet, so we add 11 and move on.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Found: 11 + -1 = 10
slides.narration: At -1 we need 11, and it's already in the set. We return 11 and -1.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We create a hash set, loop over the array, and for each value x check whether target minus x is in the set. If it is, we return the pair right away; otherwise we add x. Falling out of the loop means no pair exists.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(n)
Space: O(n) using a hash set of seen values
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is O of n using a hash set of seen values.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: No pair → return an empty array
Don't pair a number with itself (check before adding)
Negative numbers work the same way
slides.narration: If there's no pair, return an empty array. Checking the set before adding the current number guarantees we never pair a number with itself.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Mention all three approaches and their trade-offs
Follow-up: return indices; or all pairs; or 3-sum
Ask whether the input fits in memory
slides.narration: Walk through all three approaches and their trade-offs. Common follow-ups are returning indices, finding all pairs, or extending to three-number sum.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: For each number x, we need to know if its partner, target minus x, has already appeared.
Complexity: O(n)
slides.narration: To recap Two Number Sum: For each number x, we need to know if its partner, target minus x, has already appeared. A hash set answers that instantly. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
